posts.title: SGLang's Paged Experts: Giant MoE Models on One Consumer GPU
posts.subtitle: A new opt-in paging trick beats CPU offload by up to 30x
posts.summary: SGLang v0.5.23 (Nov 2, 2026) adds 'Paged Experts,' an opt-in feature that lets mixture-of-experts models bigger than a GPU's VRAM run on a single consumer card — up to 30x faster than the previous CPU-offload fallback. The same release adds fused low-latency decode kernels, Google TPU7x support, and LoRA serving on quantized MoE models.

slides.title: A Model Too Big for Your GPU. One Flag Fixes the Math.
slides.body: Mixture-of-experts models can have far more total parameters than any single consumer GPU's VRAM. SGLang's new release makes that gap survivable without a server rack.
bullets: SGLang v0.5.23 — released Nov 2, 2026
1,007 PRs, 257 contributors in this release alone

slides.title: MoE Models Outgrow Consumer GPUs by Design
slides.body: A mixture-of-experts model only activates a fraction of its experts per token, but all the experts still have to live somewhere in memory to be available.
bullets: Total parameter count (all experts combined) routinely exceeds a 16GB or 24GB consumer card's VRAM
The prior fallback, SGLang's --cpu-offload-gb flag, keeps unused experts in CPU RAM and streams them over PCIe on demand
PCIe bandwidth is the bottleneck: swapping experts in and out on every forward pass is slow enough to make the model impractical for real use

slides.title: Paged Experts: Treat Expert Weights Like OS Virtual Memory
slides.body: The new opt-in feature (PRs #42557 and #45787) pages expert weights in and out of GPU memory the way an operating system pages memory to disk — only moving what's needed, when it's needed.
bullets: Lets MoE models whose total weights don't fit in VRAM run on a single consumer GPU
Reported gain: 12x–30x faster single-stream decode versus --cpu-offload-gb on a 16GB card
Supports quantized experts out of the box: AWQ, compressed-tensors, MXFP4, NVFP4, W8A8, and block-INT8
Opt-in — existing serving setups are unaffected unless explicitly enabled

slides.title: The Rest of v0.5.23: Not Just Paging
slides.body: Paged Experts is the headline, but the release ships several other serving-focused upgrades in the same cut.
bullets: Megakernel (NVIDIA) and monokernel (AMD) fused decode kernels: up to 44% faster single-user decode on GB300, up to 75% faster on MI350X for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
SGLang-TorchTPU: a new PyTorch-native plugin adding Google TPU7x support
A new opt-in LoRA engine (PR #45892) serves LoRA adapters on quantized MoE models — specifically FP8 and NVFP4 experts

slides.title: Paged Experts vs. the Old CPU-Offload Path
slides.body: Both approaches solve the same problem — fitting a too-big MoE model on one GPU — but land in very different places on speed.

slides.title: Who This Actually Unlocks
slides.body: Picture a developer with a single RTX 4080 (16GB) who wants to experiment with a large MoE model locally.
bullets: Before: either rent a multi-GPU cluster, or use CPU offload and accept decode speeds too slow for interactive use
Now: enable Paged Experts with a quantized expert format (e.g. NVFP4), and the same model runs on that one card at up to 30x the prior offload speed
This doesn't make the GPU bigger — it makes the parts of the model that don't fit cost much less to borrow back from CPU RAM when needed

slides.title: Where It Falls Short
slides.body: Paged Experts is a real unlock, not a replacement for having enough VRAM.
bullets: Still opt-in and newly shipped — expect rough edges relative to SGLang's mature all-on-GPU path
Latency remains higher than serving a model that fits entirely in VRAM; paging still costs real PCIe transfer time, just much less of it
Built for single-stream/low-concurrency use — it is not positioned as a high-throughput multi-request production serving mode
Benefits depend on quantized expert formats being available for your specific model

slides.title: What to Remember
slides.body: SGLang v0.5.23 turns 'this MoE model is too big for my GPU' into a solvable problem for local and small-scale use.
bullets: Paged Experts: 12x–30x faster than CPU offload for oversized MoE models on a single consumer GPU, opt-in
Ships alongside megakernel/monokernel decode speedups, TPU7x support, and quantized-MoE LoRA serving
Best fit: single-user local experimentation on consumer hardware, not high-concurrency production serving
Released Nov 2, 2026 as part of a 1,007-PR release cycle

questions.prompt: What problem does SGLang's 'Paged Experts' feature solve?
options: It speeds up training of mixture-of-experts models
It lets MoE models whose total weight size exceeds a single GPU's VRAM run on that one consumer GPU
It reduces the number of experts a model needs at inference time
It compresses model weights permanently to a smaller file size
questions.explanation: Paged Experts pages expert weights between GPU and CPU memory on demand, similar to OS virtual memory, so a MoE model larger than the GPU's VRAM can still run on that single card.

questions.prompt: How does Paged Experts compare to the prior --cpu-offload-gb approach, per the release notes?
options: It's slower but uses less memory
It's roughly equivalent in speed but easier to configure
It reports 12x-30x faster single-stream decode on a 16GB card
It removes the need for any CPU memory at all
questions.explanation: The release notes report a 12x to 30x single-stream decode speedup over the previous --cpu-offload-gb flag on a 16GB GPU, since Paged Experts moves data more efficiently than the older offload path.

questions.prompt: What is Paged Experts NOT well suited for, according to its own limitations?
options: Running on consumer-grade GPUs
Quantized expert formats like NVFP4
High-throughput, high-concurrency production serving with many simultaneous requests
Single-user local experimentation
questions.explanation: The feature is described as built for single-stream, low-concurrency use — it unlocks running oversized models at all, but isn't positioned to replace fully-in-VRAM serving for high-throughput production workloads.

posts.title: vLLM v0.33.0: CUDA 13-Only Builds, Day-0 Model Support
posts.subtitle: A major open-source serving engine drops CUDA 12.9 and ships six new models on release day.
posts.summary: vLLM v0.33.0 (Nov 2) moves its official builds to CUDA 13.0 only, adds day-0 support for six-plus new models, upgrades speculative decoding with a lossy verification mode, and removes three legacy code paths. It's a snapshot of how fast open-source LLM serving infrastructure is turning over.

slides.title: vLLM v0.33.0 Lands With a Hard CUDA Cutover
slides.body: Released Nov 2, this is the third vLLM minor release in a month — and the first to require CUDA 13.0, dropping 12.9 artifacts entirely.

slides.title: Serving Infra Has to Chase Hardware and Models at Once
slides.body: A serving engine used in production has two moving targets: new accelerators (Blackwell, MI355X, GB300) that need bespoke kernels, and a flood of new open models that need day-0 support before anyone can even benchmark them.
bullets: Every new GPU generation (Blackwell, MI355X) needs its own attention/decode kernel to actually see a speedup
Each new model architecture can break existing speculative-decoding drafters built for a different shape
Carrying old CUDA/ROCm targets forever means never fully optimizing for the new ones

slides.title: What v0.33.0 Actually Ships
slides.body: The release bundles a platform bump, hardware-specific decode paths, and speculative-decoding upgrades.
bullets: Platform: upgraded to PyTorch 2.14; release wheels/images now target CUDA 13.0 only — no more CUDA 12.9 artifacts
NVIDIA: opt-in latency-specialized decode on GB300, plus FA4 sparse MLA decode on Blackwell
AMD: default ROCm build moves to ROCm 10.0, with new MonoKernel decode for several MI300X/MI355X models
Speculative decoding: new 'XPress' refiner for block-diffusion drafters, an opt-in lossy verification policy ('FLy'), and a quantized draft lm_head option
Serving API: new /v1/decisions endpoint, late-chunking support on /v1/embeddings, and a watchdog that dumps stack traces from stuck worker processes

slides.title: Three Releases, Three Different Bets
slides.body: Looking at the last month of minor releases shows the project rotating its focus rather than doing everything at once.

rows: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash perf (FlashMLA + NVFP4 KV cache) and fast-restart via weight preloading
Structured-output endpoint (/v1/systemone), low-precision KV cache rollout, Model Runner V2
CUDA 13-only platform cutover, day-0 models, speculative-decoding overhaul

slides.title: What an Upgrade Actually Looks Like
slides.body: A team running inference on a GB300 cluster, serving one of the new day-0 models (e.g. Step-5 Preview), hits two changes at once when they pull v0.33.0.
bullets: Gain: the GB300 latency-specialized decode path and FA4 sparse MLA (Blackwell) can cut per-token latency without any model change
Break: their CUDA 12.9 image no longer exists upstream — the CI pipeline must rebuild against CUDA 13.0 before the upgrade even runs
Break: if they were using Medusa or the MLP speculator for speculative decoding, that code path is gone and must be replaced with a supported drafter

slides.title: Pitfalls Before You Upgrade
slides.body: This is a breaking release, not a drop-in update.
bullets: Confirm your CI/deploy images can build against CUDA 13.0 — 12.9 artifacts are not published for this version
Medusa, the MLP speculator, and the legacy Ray compiled-graph executor are removed outright, not deprecated
AMD fleets on older ROCm should test on ROCm 10.0 before rolling this out — MonoKernel decode is new, not universal across MI-series cards
Treat each minor vLLM release as a potential breaking change: the project ships fast (three minors in a month) and doesn't hold back removals

options: It drops Python 3.10 support
Release wheels/images now target CUDA 13.0 only, with CUDA 12.9 artifacts no longer published
It removes GPU support entirely in favor of CPU inference
It switches from PyTorch to JAX
questions.explanation: v0.33.0 upgrades to PyTorch 2.14 and moves official builds to CUDA 13.0 exclusively — teams still on CUDA 12.9 images need to rebuild before upgrading.

options: Draft-model speculative decoding and custom logits processors
The GPU n-gram speculator

options: FA4 sparse MLA decode on Blackwell and MonoKernel decode on MI300X/MI355X under ROCm 10.0
Support for TPU v6
A fallback to CPU-only inference when no GPU is detected
Native support for quantum accelerators
questions.explanation: The release adds hardware-specific decode paths for both NVIDIA Blackwell (FA4 sparse MLA) and AMD's newest MI-series cards under the ROCm 10.0 default build.

posts.title: Chunking: The RAG Decision Everyone Underrates
posts.subtitle: How you cut a document up matters more than which embedding model you pick.
posts.summary: Chunking — how a document gets split before embedding — silently caps RAG recall long before the LLM sees anything. Fixed-size, recursive, semantic, and sentence-window chunking each trade off recall, cost, and complexity differently, and picking wrong hurts more than any embedding-model swap.

slides.title: The Chunk Boundary You Draw Decides What's Findable
slides.body: Split a document wrong and no embedding model, however good, can recover the signal you just threw away.

slides.title: One Vector Has to Represent a Whole Chunk
slides.body: Embedding models compress a chunk into a single fixed-size vector. Cram in too much and distinct ideas average into mush; cut it too small and you lose the context that made the passage answer the question.
bullets: A 2,000-token chunk covering five subtopics embeds as a blurry average — a query about any one subtopic matches weakly
A 50-token chunk can be too thin to retrieve at all if the matching keywords and the actual answer sit in different chunks
Most production systems land chunk size somewhere in the 200–500 token range, not because it's magic, but because it's small enough to stay topically coherent and large enough to carry real context

slides.title: Four Chunking Strategies, Four Different Bets
slides.body: Each strategy decides where to cut based on different information about the document.
bullets: Fixed-size with overlap: split every N tokens, overlap ~10–20% so an idea split across a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk
Recursive/structure-aware: split on paragraph breaks first, then sentences, then words only as a last resort — keeps natural units intact
Semantic chunking: embed sentences, then cut where embedding similarity between consecutive sentences drops sharply — follows topic shifts, not token counts
Sentence-window: retrieve on a small chunk (1–2 sentences) for precision, but send the LLM a wider window around it for context — decouples what you match on from what you feed the model

slides.title: Picking a Strategy by What You're Optimizing For

rows: Markdown, code docs, anything with real structure
Long docs that wander across subtopics
Precise fact lookup where the exact sentence matters

slides.title: Same Pipeline, Two Documents, Two Right Answers
slides.body: A 40-page API reference and a customer-support call transcript don't want the same chunker.
bullets: API reference: recursive/structure-aware chunking that respects headers and code blocks — splitting a code sample mid-block makes it useless even if the surrounding prose is intact
Support transcript: sentence-window chunking — a customer's one-line complaint is the retrieval target, but the agent's resolution two turns later is what the LLM actually needs to answer with
Using fixed-size chunking on either would occasionally slice a code block in half or separate a question from its answer purely by token-count coincidence

slides.title: Where Chunking Goes Wrong
bullets: Overlap set too high (>30%) bloats the index and returns near-duplicate chunks that crowd out genuinely different results
Fixed-size chunking with no structural awareness will split tables, code blocks, and numbered steps mid-way — the chunk retrieves but reads as nonsense
Semantic chunking isn't free: it costs an embedding call per sentence at ingest time, which matters at large corpus scale
There's no universal best chunk size — tune it against your own retrieval eval (recall@k), not a blog post's default

questions.prompt: Why does cramming a 2,000-token chunk covering five subtopics into one embedding hurt retrieval?
options: Embedding models can't process chunks that long
The single vector ends up as a blurry average of all five subtopics, so a query about any one of them matches weakly
It makes the vector database run out of storage
It triggers a token-limit error at query time
questions.explanation: A chunk's embedding is one fixed-size vector — the more unrelated content it has to represent, the less precisely it represents any single part of it.

questions.prompt: What does sentence-window chunking decouple?
options: The embedding model from the vector database
What you match on (a small, precise unit) from what you feed the LLM (a wider context window around it)
Training data from inference data
The chunk size from the overlap percentage
questions.explanation: Sentence-window retrieval matches on a narrow 1–2 sentence unit for precision, then expands to surrounding sentences only after retrieval, giving the LLM enough context to actually answer.

questions.prompt: What's the main downside of semantic chunking?
options: It can't handle markdown or code
It requires an embedding call per sentence at ingest time, adding real cost at corpus scale
It only works with one specific embedding model
It always produces chunks larger than fixed-size chunking
questions.explanation: Semantic chunking decides boundaries by comparing sentence-level embeddings, which means extra embedding calls during ingestion — a real cost tradeoff against its better topic coherence.

posts.title: TokenEconomizer: Trimming Coding Agent Costs by 31%
posts.subtitle: A black-box plugin that prunes stale tools and caches lessons learned — no model changes required.
posts.summary: TokenEconomizer sits between a coding agent and its model, pruning unused tools and caching repo-specific lessons across sessions. On SWE-Bench it cut cost 18-31% across five agent-model combinations while mostly holding or improving task success — proof that a lot of agent spend is redundant context, not reasoning.

slides.title: Every Agent Session Starts From Zero
slides.body: Claude Code, Codex, and Copilot CLI all re-send the same tool schemas and relearn the same repo quirks on every single run — and every token costs money.

slides.title: Tool Definitions Alone Can Cost More Than the Task
bullets: Every system prompt reloads the full set of tool schemas, whether the agent needs them or not
A coding agent might carry 20+ tools for a task that only ever touches three of them
Repeated across hundreds of sessions on the same repo, that's pure waste — and it compounds on every single turn

slides.title: Three Mechanisms, Zero Changes to the Model
bullets: Micro-skills: repo facts (build command, test quirks) get written down once confirmed across 3 sessions, then stated upfront instead of rediscovered
Tool pruning: a tool unused for 10 prompts across 2+ sessions (or 5 sessions of any length) drops out of the schema — one command restores it
Failure-loop intervention: a judge model watches for an agent stuck repeating the same failed move and injects a redirect, without ever stopping the turn itself

slides.title: 18-31% Cheaper, Mostly Without Losing Accuracy
bullets: Measured on SWE-Bench across 30 repository x agent-model combinations
Cheaper in all 30 cells; Pass@1 (task success) rose in 4 of the 5 agent-model combinations

slides.title: A Repo the Agent Has Seen Before
slides.body: On session one, the agent discovers that `make test` needs ENV=ci set or it hangs. By session four, TokenEconomizer has promoted that into a micro-skill: the agent is told upfront, skipping the trial-and-error loop that burned tokens in sessions one through three.

slides.title: Where the Savings Can Backfire
bullets: Cold-start repos see no benefit yet — micro-skills only kick in after 3 confirmed sessions
A wrongly-pruned tool mid-task still forces an extra round-trip to restore it
The judge model that detects failure loops adds its own token cost — net savings assume it fires rarely
One of five combinations (Copilot CLI + Sonnet 5) saw Pass@1 drop by 1.0 point — cheaper isn't always strictly better

slides.title: A Black Box Around the Agent, Not Inside It
bullets: Sits between the agent harness and the model API, rewriting the context window — never touches model weights
Works today with Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Pi; opencode and Cursor Agent support is experimental
Open source under Apache 2.0, published by Microsoft Research

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Most coding-agent cost isn't the reasoning step — it's redundant context: tool schemas and rediscovered repo facts
A thin caching/pruning layer outside the model cut cost 18-31% with no fine-tuning in these measurements
The pattern generalizes: any agent harness re-sending static context on every call is a candidate for the same trick

posts.title: Mamba: Sequence Modeling Without Quadratic Attention
posts.subtitle: A selective state-space layer that scales linearly with sequence length — no attention matrix required.
posts.summary: Mamba replaces self-attention with a selective state-space recurrence: a fixed-size hidden state updated in parallel, giving linear-time compute and constant memory per generated token. It trades away some of attention's exact recall for dramatically cheaper long-context processing, which is why most deployed long-context models hybridize the two rather than picking one.

slides.title: Attention Isn't the Only Way to Model a Sequence
slides.body: Transformers compare every token to every other token. Mamba instead carries a compressed running state forward, token by token — closer to how an RNN works, but fast enough to compete with attention.

slides.title: Attention's Bill Grows Quadratically
bullets: Self-attention computes an N x N score matrix — double the sequence length, quadruple the compute and memory
The KV cache that stores past keys/values grows linearly with every generated token, eating GPU memory on long outputs
Recurrent nets (RNNs/LSTMs) scale linearly but train slowly — they can't be parallelized across time the way attention can

slides.title: A Selective State That Updates in Parallel
bullets: Mamba keeps a fixed-size hidden state per layer and updates it with a linear recurrence — cost per token is constant, not growing with context
The 'selective' part: input-dependent gating lets the model decide, per token, how much of the past state to keep vs. overwrite — plain state-space models like S4 can't do this
A hardware-aware parallel scan algorithm computes the recurrence across the whole sequence at once on GPU, instead of looping token by token

slides.title: Linear Time, Constant Memory Per Step
A 200-Page Document, Summarized Token by Token
slides.body: Feed a 200-page contract through a Transformer and the attention matrix needs memory proportional to the square of the token count — long documents force chunking or truncation. A Mamba-based model instead walks through the contract once, continuously compressing everything read so far into a fixed-size state, then generates a summary with no growing cache.

slides.title: Where Mamba Struggles
bullets: Exact retrieval is weaker: 'what was the 3rd number mentioned on page 40?' is easy for attention's direct lookups, hard for a compressed state that may have overwritten it
Pure state-space models lag transformers on in-context learning and copying tasks in published benchmarks
Most production systems hedge with hybrids — architectures like Jamba interleave Mamba layers with a few attention layers to keep precise recall where it matters

slides.title: Where It Fits Today
bullets: Best suited for very long contexts where attention's memory cost is the bottleneck: genomics, audio, long documents
Hybrid architectures (Mamba plus sparse attention) are more common in deployed models than pure state-space models
Same training recipes (next-token prediction, RLHF/DPO) apply — it's a drop-in architecture change, not a new training paradigm

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Mamba trades attention's exact, quadratic lookups for a compressed, linear-time running state
That trade wins decisively on raw long-context throughput and memory, and loses on precise recall
The practical answer for most production models isn't 'replace attention' — it's a hybrid that uses each where it's strongest

questions.prompt: Why does a Transformer's self-attention get expensive on long sequences?
options: It needs more training data
The attention score matrix grows quadratically with sequence length
It requires more GPUs for identical throughput
It can only process one token at a time
questions.explanation: Every token attends to every other token, so an N-token sequence needs an N x N score matrix — compute and memory both grow with the square of N.

questions.prompt: What makes Mamba 'selective' compared to earlier state-space models like S4?
options: It uses attention internally
Its state update is input-dependent, letting the model decide what to keep or discard per token
It only processes selected tokens and skips the rest
It requires manual feature selection before training
questions.explanation: Plain state-space models use fixed, input-independent dynamics. Mamba's gating lets the update depend on the current token, which is what lets it compete with attention on language tasks.

questions.prompt: Why do many production long-context models combine Mamba layers with some attention layers instead of using Mamba alone?
options: Pure Mamba models are too slow to train
Attention is required for the model to be differentiable
Mamba's compressed state is weaker at exact recall, so a few attention layers recover precise lookups
Mamba can't run on GPUs
questions.explanation: Mamba's fixed-size state can't perfectly preserve every past token the way attention's direct lookups can, so hybrids like Jamba keep a few attention layers for tasks that need exact recall.

posts.title: Quantization: Shrinking LLMs by Rounding Their Weights
posts.subtitle: Store weights in 4 or 8 bits instead of 16, and a 70B model suddenly fits on one GPU.
posts.summary: Quantization compresses a trained model's weights from 16-bit floats down to 8-bit or 4-bit integers, cutting memory and bandwidth needs by 2-4x with only a small, often-recoverable quality cost. Modern post-training methods like GPTQ and AWQ make this practical without retraining the whole model, which is why it's the default trick for running big LLMs on smaller hardware.

slides.title: Why a 70B Model Doesn't Need 32 Bits Per Weight
slides.body: Every weight in a neural network is just a number. Quantization asks: do we really need 16 or 32 bits of precision to store it, or would 8 or even 4 bits do almost as well?
bullets: A 70B-parameter model in FP16 needs ~140GB of memory just for weights
Quantized to INT4, the same weights fit in roughly 35-40GB — small enough for a single high-end consumer GPU
The technique is central to 'inference optimization': it shrinks cost and latency, not training time

slides.title: The Memory Wall: Compute Is Cheap, Moving Weights Isn't
slides.body: Modern GPUs can do trillions of operations per second, but inference is often bottlenecked by moving weights from GPU memory to the compute cores, not by the math itself.
bullets: Autoregressive decoding generates one token at a time, re-reading the entire weight matrix from memory for every single token
Smaller weights mean less data to move per step, which directly speeds up token generation on memory-bandwidth-bound hardware
Big models also need more GPUs just to hold weights in VRAM, before a single request is served — fewer GPUs needed means lower cost per request

slides.title: From Floats to Integers: Scale, Round, Store
slides.body: At its core, quantization maps a range of floating-point values to a small set of integers using a scale factor (and sometimes a zero-point offset), then reverses the mapping at compute time.
bullets: Per-tensor quantization uses one scale for a whole weight matrix; per-channel or per-group quantization uses many smaller scales for better accuracy
Post-training quantization (PTQ) — methods like GPTQ and AWQ — quantizes an already-trained model using a small calibration dataset, no retraining required
GPTQ quantizes weights layer-by-layer, adjusting remaining unquantized weights to compensate for the error just introduced — this is what keeps 4-bit models usably accurate
AWQ instead identifies the small fraction of 'salient' weight channels most sensitive to error (tied to large activation magnitudes) and protects those specifically

slides.title: Precision Formats: The Memory/Quality Tradeoff
slides.body: Roughly how precision choice affects a model's footprint and typical quality impact (actual numbers vary by model and method):
bullets: FP16 is the common training/serving baseline; INT8 is close to a free lunch for most models
INT4 with a good calibration method (GPTQ/AWQ) usually stays close to FP16 quality on most benchmarks, but the gap widens on tasks needing precise numerical or multi-step reasoning

slides.title: Worked Example: Fitting a 70B Model on One GPU
slides.body: A team wants to self-host a 70B open-weight model for internal tooling but only has a single 48GB GPU.
bullets: In FP16, the weights alone (~140GB) can't even load — they'd need 4+ high-memory GPUs just for storage
Quantized to 4-bit with AWQ, the weights shrink to ~35-40GB, leaving headroom for the KV cache and fitting on one card
They run a quick calibration pass (a few hundred representative prompts) so the quantizer knows which activation channels matter most before compressing
Result: one GPU serves the model at a modest quality cost, instead of needing a multi-GPU cluster for the same workload

slides.title: Pitfalls and When Not to Quantize
slides.body: Quantization isn't free, and pushing it too far or applying it carelessly can quietly break a model in ways standard benchmarks miss.
bullets: Outlier activations (a small number of unusually large values) are the main source of quantization error — methods that ignore them degrade badly at low bit-widths
Aggregate benchmark scores can look fine while specific capabilities (precise arithmetic, long-context recall, rare-but-critical edge cases) quietly degrade
Calibration data that doesn't match real traffic (e.g. calibrating on English text, deploying on code) can quantize the wrong channels well and the wrong ones poorly
Below ~3-4 bits, quality loss tends to grow sharply — most production deployments stop at INT4 or INT8 rather than going lower
Hardware/kernel support matters: a quantization format is only as fast as the inference engine's kernels for it — not every format is accelerated on every GPU

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Quantization trades a small, often-manageable amount of accuracy for large, reliable savings in memory and serving cost.
bullets: INT8 is close to free; INT4 needs a good calibration method (GPTQ, AWQ) to stay accurate
The real bottleneck it solves is memory bandwidth during token-by-token decoding, not raw compute
Always validate on your actual task distribution, not just aggregate benchmarks — quality loss can be uneven across capabilities
It's a serving-time optimization, complementary to (not a replacement for) techniques like KV-cache compression or speculative decoding

questions.prompt: What is the primary bottleneck that weight quantization addresses during LLM inference?
options: The number of floating-point operations the GPU can perform per second
Memory bandwidth — moving weights from memory to compute cores for every generated token
The size of the training dataset used to pretrain the model
Network latency between the client and the server
questions.explanation: Autoregressive decoding re-reads the full weight matrix for every token generated, so inference is often memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound. Smaller (quantized) weights mean less data to move per step, which speeds up generation.

questions.prompt: Why do methods like GPTQ and AWQ use a small calibration dataset instead of just rounding every weight independently?
options: To retrain the entire model from scratch on new data
To measure which weights/channels matter most for real outputs, so errors can be minimized or compensated for where it counts
To generate synthetic training data for the next model version
Calibration data is required by law for releasing open-weight models
questions.explanation: Naive rounding treats every weight equally, but errors aren't equally costly. GPTQ compensates remaining weights for error introduced earlier in the same layer; AWQ protects the specific channels tied to large activations. Both use a small calibration set to find what actually matters — neither retrains the model.

questions.prompt: A team quantizes a model to INT4 and sees nearly identical scores on standard benchmarks, but users report the model suddenly makes more arithmetic mistakes. What's the most likely explanation?
options: INT4 quantization always improves reasoning performance
The benchmark suite doesn't cover the capability that degraded, even though aggregate scores look fine
This is impossible — quantization cannot affect specific capabilities
The GPU hardware is defective
questions.explanation: Quality loss from quantization is often uneven: broad benchmarks can look stable while precise, low-tolerance capabilities like multi-step arithmetic degrade more than average. This is why the pitfalls slide stresses validating on your actual task distribution, not just aggregate scores.

posts.title: Claude Haiku 5.5: 75% Cheaper, Built for Agent Fleets
posts.subtitle: Anthropic's smallest model gets an effort dial, a steep price cut, and a job as every bigger model's subagent.
posts.summary: Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 is its fastest and cheapest model yet, costing roughly 75% less than Haiku 4.5 while adding its first adjustable effort setting and a role as a subagent for Opus and Sonnet on coding tasks. It jumps dramatically over Haiku 4.5 on every reported benchmark but still trails Sonnet 5.5 badly on hard reasoning.

slides.title: A Small Model Built to Run at Fleet Scale
slides.body: Released October 7, 2026 as the fifth model in the Claude 5.5 family, after Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5.
bullets: About 75% cheaper than Haiku 4.5 on average: $0.10/M input, $0.50/M output tokens (prompts up to 100K)
Anthropic's fastest model at standard speed, meant for summaries, classification, and live support
First Haiku model with an adjustable effort dial, from Low to Max

slides.title: Why a Cheaper, Dumber Model Is the Real Scaling Bottleneck
slides.body: Most production AI traffic isn't a hard reasoning question — it's summarization, classification, and routine subagent calls repeated millions of times, where token price matters more than ceiling intelligence.
bullets: Sonnet 5.5 costs 20x more per input token than Haiku 5.5 ($2.00 vs $0.10 per 1M, ≤100K context)
Agent systems increasingly delegate narrow subtasks to a cheap model instead of calling the flagship for everything

slides.title: What Actually Changed: An Effort Dial, Not Just a Price Cut

bullets: Effort levels: Low, Medium, High, Xhigh, Max — same model, different latency/quality tradeoff per call
Runs as a subagent alongside Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 on coding tasks, not just as a standalone chat model
Uses an updated tokenizer that spends slightly more tokens per task than Haiku 4.5

slides.title: Big Jump Over Haiku 4.5, Still Well Behind Sonnet 5.5

posts.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration: Supervisor vs. Swarm
posts.subtitle: When one agent isn't enough, how you wire many together matters more than which model you pick.
posts.summary: Multi-agent orchestration splits one task across specialized agents instead of one agent doing everything — the supervisor, hierarchical, swarm, and blackboard patterns each trade off control, cost, and debuggability differently. It beats a monolithic agent on specialization and parallelism, but multiplies token spend and adds coordination risk, so it's worth reaching for only once a single well-prompted agent has actually failed.

slides.title: One Agent Hits a Wall. Multiple Agents Hit a Coordination Problem.
slides.body: Multi-agent orchestration is the set of patterns for splitting one open-ended task across several specialized LLM agents instead of asking one agent to do everything.
bullets: Used by LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, and Claude's own subagent tooling to split work across roles
The design choice that matters most isn't which model to use — it's how agents are organized and who's in control
More agents means more cost, more latency, and more ways for a task to silently go wrong

slides.title: Why One Big Agent Eventually Breaks Down
slides.body: A single agent juggling research, coding, and review in one context window accumulates irrelevant history, loses track of its own goal, and burns tokens re-reading things it already decided.
bullets: Context windows fill with tool output from unrelated subtasks, diluting attention on what matters right now
One failure — a bad tool call, a hallucinated fact — can derail the rest of the task with no checkpoint to recover from
A monolithic agent can't specialize: the same model and prompt handle planning, coding, and QA equally (and equally badly)

slides.title: The Supervisor Pattern: One Agent Delegates, Others Execute
slides.body: A supervisor agent breaks the task into subtasks, assigns each to a specialized worker, and assembles their results — the most common production pattern today.
bullets: Workers only see their own subtask, not the full conversation — smaller, cleaner context per agent
The supervisor can retry, reassign, or skip a failed worker without restarting the whole task
Easiest pattern to debug: there's one place, the supervisor, that holds the overall plan

slides.title: Beyond Supervisor: Hierarchical and Peer-to-Peer Swarms
slides.body: A single supervisor doesn't scale to very large workflows alone — three other patterns fill the gaps.
bullets: Hierarchical: supervisors-of-supervisors, each managing a team of workers, used when one supervisor's context can't hold the whole plan
Swarm / handoff: agents pass control directly to whichever agent is best suited next, with no fixed coordinator
Blackboard: agents don't talk to each other at all — they read and write a shared memory store, and whichever agent's trigger condition matches acts next

slides.title: Which Pattern, When
slides.body: Pick based on how predictable the workflow is and how much you need a single point of control.

rows: Supervisor becomes a bottleneck or context hog
Hard to trace who decided what, harder to debug
Many agents reacting to shared state
Race conditions, no clear owner of the final decision

slides.title: A Concrete Walkthrough: Automated Code Review
slides.body: A supervisor agent receives a pull request diff and splits review into three worker calls run in parallel, then merges their findings into one report.
bullets: Worker A (security): scans only the diff for injection, auth, and secrets issues — a few thousand tokens of context, not the whole repo
Worker B (correctness): checks the diff's logic against the PR description and existing tests
Worker C (style): checks the diff against the repo's lint config
Supervisor merges three short reports into one, deduplicating overlapping findings — far cheaper than one agent reading the whole repo for every concern

slides.title: The Tradeoffs Nobody Puts in the Demo
slides.body: Multi-agent systems trade single-agent simplicity for coordination cost, and that cost is easy to underestimate.
bullets: Cost multiplies: 5 worker agents means roughly 5x the token spend of one agent working sequentially, even with smaller per-worker context
Latency can get worse, not better, if workers run sequentially instead of in parallel — orchestration adds round-trips
Shared state without a clear owner (blackboard, swarm handoffs) is a common source of silent task failure — nobody notices that no one actually finished the job
Rule of thumb: don't reach for multi-agent until a single well-prompted agent with good tools has actually failed on the task

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Multi-agent orchestration splits one task across specialized agents — the pattern (supervisor, hierarchical, swarm, blackboard) matters more than the model choice
Supervisor is the default: one agent plans and delegates, workers execute with narrow context, the supervisor merges results
It costs more in tokens and latency than a single agent — use it when specialization or parallelism actually pays for that overhead, not by default

questions.prompt: In the supervisor pattern, what's the main advantage over one large monolithic agent?
options: Each worker agent gets a smaller, focused context instead of the entire task history
It uses a completely different, cheaper model automatically
It eliminates the need for tool use
It guarantees lower latency in all cases
questions.explanation: Workers only see their own subtask, which keeps their context clean and focused — the supervisor holds the overall plan and merges results, but latency and cost aren't automatically improved.

questions.prompt: Which pattern lets agents hand off control directly to each other with no fixed coordinator?
options: Swarm / peer-to-peer handoff
Supervisor
Hierarchical
Blackboard
questions.explanation: Swarm or peer-to-peer handoff designs let any agent pass control directly to whichever agent is best suited next, without a central supervisor making that call.

questions.prompt: What's the most common hidden cost of adding more agents to a workflow?
options: Token spend multiplies even when each agent's individual context is smaller
Agents automatically get smarter
The workflow becomes easier to debug
Context windows become irrelevant
questions.explanation: More agents means more separate LLM calls — even if each one has a smaller, focused context, the total token spend across all of them is usually higher than one well-prompted agent doing the work sequentially.

posts.title: Reflexion: Agents That Learn From Their Own Mistakes
posts.subtitle: No gradient update, no fine-tuning — just a written note the agent reads before trying again
posts.summary: Reflexion adds a verbal self-critique loop on top of an acting agent: after a failed attempt, a separate reflection step writes down what went wrong in plain language, and that note gets added to the agent's context on the next try. It is cheap, needs no weight updates, but only works when there is a clear pass/fail signal to react to.

slides.title: An Agent That Repeats the Same Mistake Forever
slides.body: A standard ReAct-style agent that fails a task just tries again the same way — nothing about the attempt changes, because nothing about its state changed. Reflexion fixes that by giving the agent a memory of its own failures, written in plain English.
bullets: From Shinn et al., 'Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning'
Learning happens in the prompt, not in the weights

slides.title: Retrying Isn't Learning
slides.body: Give a tool-using agent a second attempt after it fails, and by default it brings nothing from the first attempt except the same prompt and the same weights.
bullets: No gradient update happens between attempts — the policy is frozen
Without an explicit record of the failure, the next rollout can make the exact same wrong call
Environments like coding, games, and multi-step QA give a reward signal (pass/fail) but no explanation of *why* it failed
Fine-tuning on failures is possible but slow, expensive, and overkill for a single task instance

slides.title: Three Roles: Actor, Evaluator, Self-Reflection
slides.body: Reflexion splits the loop into three parts that run in sequence after each attempt.
bullets: Actor: the agent itself — generates the trajectory of thoughts/actions (e.g. a ReAct loop) that attempts the task
Evaluator: scores the outcome — a unit test suite, a game's win/loss signal, or exact-match on a QA answer
Self-Reflection model: given the failed trajectory and the evaluator's verdict, writes a short natural-language diagnosis of what went wrong and what to try differently
That reflection text is appended to an episodic memory buffer and injected into the Actor's context on the next attempt

slides.title: Example: A Failed Coding Attempt, Retried
slides.body: Task: write a function that returns the second-largest number in a list.
bullets: Attempt 1: agent writes code that assumes the list always has 2+ distinct values — fails the test case [5, 5, 5]
Evaluator: unit test fails, reports which test case broke
Self-Reflection: 'My solution assumed the two largest values are distinct. I need to handle duplicate values by tracking the second-largest distinct value explicitly.'
Attempt 2: Actor reads that reflection in context, rewrites the function to track distinct values, passes all tests

slides.title: Plain Retry vs. Reflexion vs. Fine-Tuning
slides.body: Each way of 'learning from failure' trades off cost, speed, and how much it generalizes.

rows: A written diagnosis in episodic memory, read as context
One extra inference call (the reflection) per failed attempt
A full training run — far more compute, and not instance-specific

slides.title: Where It Breaks Down
slides.body: Reflexion depends entirely on having something concrete to react to.
bullets: Needs a clear evaluator signal — easy for unit tests or game win/loss, much harder for open-ended or subjective tasks with no automatic scorer
Each failed attempt burns a full extra rollout plus a reflection call — costly if the task allows many retries
An unbounded memory buffer can accumulate stale or contradictory reflections across many attempts, confusing later ones
It fixes mistakes within a task instance — it does not transfer what it learned to a completely different task the way fine-tuning would

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Reflexion = Actor (acts) + Evaluator (scores) + Self-Reflection (writes a lesson), looped across attempts
The 'learning' lives in a growing text memory the agent reads, not in updated weights
Works best on tasks with a crisp pass/fail signal and a bounded number of retries
Cheaper and faster to iterate than fine-tuning, but doesn't generalize beyond the current task instance

questions.prompt: In Reflexion, what actually changes between a failed attempt and the next retry?
options: The model's weights are fine-tuned on the failure
A written self-reflection is added to context so the Actor sees what went wrong
The task is simplified automatically
The Evaluator is swapped for a stricter one
questions.explanation: Reflexion never touches model weights — the Self-Reflection step writes a natural-language diagnosis of the failure, and that text is added to the Actor's context on the next attempt. The 'learning' is entirely in-context.

questions.prompt: Why can't Reflexion be used on just any task?
options: It only works with language models larger than 100B parameters
It requires a clear evaluator signal (pass/fail, win/loss) to know a reflection is even needed
It can only be used with search-tool agents
It requires access to the model's training data
questions.explanation: The whole loop starts from the Evaluator's verdict. Without a concrete signal that the attempt failed (and ideally why), there's nothing for the Self-Reflection step to diagnose — which is why Reflexion fits unit-tested code or scored games far better than open-ended, subjective tasks.

questions.prompt: Compared to fine-tuning on failed trajectories, what's the main tradeoff of Reflexion?
options: Reflexion is slower but produces a model that generalizes better
Reflexion is cheap and fast per task instance, but the lesson doesn't transfer to a different task
Reflexion requires labeled training data while fine-tuning does not
There is no meaningful difference between the two
questions.explanation: Reflexion only costs an extra inference call per failed attempt and needs no training run, but its 'memory' is scoped to the current task instance — move to a new task and that learned lesson doesn't come along, unlike a weight update from fine-tuning.

posts.title: DPO: Skipping the Reward Model Entirely
posts.subtitle: One classification loss replaces reward modeling and PPO.
posts.summary: Direct Preference Optimization reframes RLHF as a single classification loss over preference pairs, skipping the separate reward model and PPO loop entirely. It's simpler and more stable to train, and now sits behind alignment in many open-weight model releases — though it inherits its own failure modes, like length bias and sensitivity to the reference model.

slides.title: RLHF Used to Need Two Models and a Fragile RL Loop
slides.body: Classic RLHF trains a reward model from human preferences, then runs PPO against it. A 2023 Stanford paper collapsed both stages into one supervised loss.
bullets: Old recipe: reward model, then an on-policy RL loop to optimize against it
New recipe: one loss function, computed directly from preference pairs
Paper: Rafailov et al., 'Direct Preference Optimization' (arXiv:2305.18290)

slides.title: Classic RLHF Is Expensive and Unstable
slides.body: Standard RLHF fits a separate reward model on labeled preference data, then optimizes the policy against that reward with PPO — an on-policy RL algorithm that needs live rollouts, a value network, and careful KL-penalty tuning.
bullets: Two full training stages: reward model, then RL fine-tuning
PPO needs sampling, a value head, and a KL coefficient — many knobs to get wrong
If the policy drifts too far from the reward model's training distribution, it can exploit the reward model (classic reward hacking)

slides.title: The Trick: the Optimal Policy Has a Closed Form
slides.body: For the usual RLHF objective (maximize reward, stay close to a reference model under a KL penalty), the optimal policy can be written directly as a function of the reward. Substituting that relationship into the Bradley-Terry preference model produces a loss defined purely on the policy — no separate reward model needed.
bullets: Implicit reward = beta times the log-ratio of policy probability to reference-model probability
Loss = binary cross-entropy: raise the log-probability of the chosen response, lower it for the rejected one
Only needs a frozen reference model (usually the SFT checkpoint) plus preference pairs — no reward model, no rollouts

slides.title: Worked Example: One Preference Pair, One Update
slides.body: Prompt: 'Explain photosynthesis to a 5-year-old.' Response A (simple, chosen by the labeler) and response B (jargon-heavy, rejected) come from the same prompt.
bullets: Compute log pi(A) minus log pi_ref(A), and log pi(B) minus log pi_ref(B)
Take the difference between those two margins, scale by beta, pass through a sigmoid — that's the per-example loss
If the policy already favors A over B more than the reference model does, the gradient is small
If the policy still favors B, the gradient pushes hard to flip that preference
Beta controls how far the policy is allowed to drift from the reference model while doing this

slides.title: DPO vs. PPO-Based RLHF
slides.body: Each approach gets to the same KL-constrained objective, but through very different machinery.

rows: Live rollouts scored by the reward model
Sensitive to the KL coefficient; can collapse
A standard supervised classification loss — far steadier
Reward-model training, then an RL sampling loop
Reward hacking if KL control slips
Length/verbosity bias; depends on reference-model quality

slides.title: Where DPO Breaks: Length Bias and Reference Drift
slides.body: Because the implicit reward is just a log-probability ratio, a policy can raise its score by making chosen-style responses longer or more hedged without actually being better — and human annotators often do prefer longer answers, so DPO inherits that bias from the data.
bullets: Needs same-prompt chosen/rejected PAIRS — it can't train on isolated ratings the way a reward model can
Verbosity bias: longer isn't better, but DPO will learn that correlation if it's in the preference data
A weak or mismatched reference model gives DPO nothing good to anchor its updates to
Newer variants try to fix this: KTO drops the paired-data requirement, ORPO drops the reference model entirely

slides.title: DPO Collapsed RLHF Into a Fine-Tuning Recipe
slides.body: The core move: derive the optimal RLHF policy in closed form, then optimize for it directly with a classification loss instead of simulating the whole RL loop.
bullets: One loss over preference pairs replaces a reward model plus a PPO loop
The 'reward' is implicit — a beta-scaled log-ratio between the policy and a frozen reference model
Simpler and more stable than PPO-based RLHF, but it inherits whatever biases are in the preference data
Now a common default alignment step, alongside PPO and newer methods like KTO and ORPO

questions.prompt: What does DPO eliminate from the standard RLHF pipeline?
options: The need for any human preference data
The separate reward-model training stage and the on-policy PPO loop
The frozen reference model
The language model's pretraining stage
questions.explanation: DPO still needs human preference data and a reference model. What it removes is the separate reward-model stage and the on-policy PPO loop, replacing both with one supervised classification loss.

questions.prompt: In DPO's loss, what plays the role of the 'reward' for a given response?
options: The raw output of a trained reward model
A beta-scaled log-probability ratio between the current policy and a frozen reference model
The human annotator's numeric rating of that response
The KL divergence between two separate policies
questions.explanation: By solving for the optimal policy of the standard KL-constrained RLHF objective in closed form, DPO can rewrite the reward implicitly as beta times the log-ratio of the policy's probability to the reference model's probability for that response.

questions.prompt: Why can DPO-tuned models develop a verbosity bias?
options: The loss function explicitly rewards longer responses
DPO just fits whatever pattern is in the preference pairs, and annotators often favor longer answers
The frozen reference model only ever produces long text
PPO's value network favors longer rollouts
questions.explanation: DPO has no built-in notion of length — it fits the preference data it's given. If annotators systematically preferred longer responses when labeling, the model learns that correlation as a shortcut.

posts.title: Google's Gemini Agent: One Agent, Every Job
posts.subtitle: A universal work agent that picks its own model — including Claude — and spins up sub-agents on demand.
posts.summary: Google Cloud introduced the Gemini agent, a single universal agent for chat, knowledge work, media, and code that routes each job to whichever model fits best — Gemini or Claude — and can spin up temporary sub-agents or persistent 'coworker' agents with their own identities. Governance comes from cryptographic agent identity, audit trails, sandboxing, and real-time spend caps.

slides.title: One Agent Is Supposed to Replace Your Agent Zoo
slides.body: At Gemini at Work 2026, Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian introduced the Gemini agent: one interface for chat, knowledge work, content and media generation, and writing and running code.
bullets: "Work now starts in the prompt window" — you give it objectives, not step-by-step instructions
Runs on web, iOS, Android, Windows, Mac, the command line, Workspace, Microsoft 365, or Slack
Can also run headless, embedded inside third-party apps

slides.title: Enterprises Already Have Too Many Single-Purpose Bots
slides.body: Kurian frames the real bottleneck for enterprise AI adoption as organizational, not technical: companies are past the pilot stage, but every narrow bot adds its own integration, its own risk surface, and its own bill.
bullets: The post names the two things that make or break an agent rollout: "whether you can govern it, and whether you can afford it"
Dozens of fragmented chatbots means dozens of places to audit, patch, and pay for
A single agent with one API and one identity model is the proposed fix

slides.title: It Picks the Model — Gemini or Claude — Per Job
slides.body: The Gemini agent is explicitly decoupled from any one model. A routing layer called Smart Routing sends each piece of work to whichever model is cheapest and strongest for that specific task.
bullets: Orchestrates "across our Gemini family of models and Claude models from Anthropic today, and other leading private and open models in the future"
Named Google models: Argon (frontier reasoning), Flash (speed/volume), Omni (generative media), Gemma (lightweight edge)
Smart Routing "automatically triages enterprise workloads so each one runs on the model that delivers maximum performance at the lowest possible cost"

slides.title: Sub-Agents for a Task, Coworker Agents for a Role
slides.body: Two different agent lifetimes solve two different problems.
bullets: Sub-agents: temporary, job-specific agents the main agent spins up on its own to split a multi-step task into parallel or sequential pieces that can run for hours or days
Coworker agents: persistent, role-based team members that get their own @agents.company.com email, calendar, Drive, and a listing in the company directory — acting under their own identity, not yours
Coworker agents only see the context you or your team explicitly give them

slides.title: Example: Scheduling Without Naming a Single Person
slides.body: Google's own walkthrough: inside Workspace, you ask Gemini to "schedule a meeting with the usual team of regional event leads next week" — without supplying a single name or email address.
bullets: Gemini resolves "usual team of regional event leads" from its semantic memory of how your org actually works, not a hardcoded list
A data engineer can instead ask it to generate PySpark code, hand back an editable notebook, train a model, and self-fix pipeline errors
A business user can save an operational report once, then rerun it on demand against BigQuery with zero added token cost

slides.title: Four Kinds of Memory, Not One Chat History
slides.body: Rather than a single growing transcript, the agent keeps four distinct memory types so long-running work doesn't collapse into one undifferentiated context window.
bullets: Session memory: the current task, even if it runs for days
Semantic memory: a structured knowledge base built from documents, conversations, and other agents
Procedural memory: how a job gets done, including skills the agent writes for itself
Episodic memory: a record of everything it has done before

slides.title: The Numbers Are Vendor-Reported Customer Results
slides.body: Google's post backs the launch with specific customer figures — useful context, but all self-reported by Google and its customers, not independently audited.
bullets: Treat these as directional claims from the vendor's own announcement, not third-party benchmarks

rows: Document review time: 1 hour → 5 minutes; risk inconsistencies down 60%
SQL query accuracy up 63% during initial development
Routes 10 million multi-model requests per week

slides.title: Governance Is the Pitch — and the Catch
slides.body: The post leans hard on control features, which also hints at where this is still early.
bullets: Every agent gets a cryptographically attested identity with least-privilege, role-based permissions and a full audit trail attributed to the agent, not a person
Agents run inside an Agent Sandbox with its own network boundary, behind an Agent Gateway that enforces policy (e.g. "agents may not open documents classified Need to Know")
Teams can set a hard AI spend cap per project in Cloud Billing; hitting it pauses that project's agent until someone clicks resume

Caveat: Google's post never states a general-availability date for the core Gemini agent — only its Financial Services and Legal specializations are explicitly in preview, with Government, Healthcare, and Retail "coming soon"

slides.title: One API, Many Models, Real Guardrails
slides.body: The Gemini agent's bet is that enterprises don't want more model choice — they want one surface that routes between models and never loses track of who (or what) did what.
bullets: Model-agnostic by design: Gemini and Claude run side-by-side under one router today
Two agent lifetimes — ephemeral sub-agents for tasks, persistent coworker agents for roles — map cleanly onto how real teams delegate work
The open question is adoption proof beyond Google's own customer anecdotes, and when the core agent itself leaves preview

questions.explanation: Spend caps are enforced per project: once the cap is hit, that project's agent pauses, and work resumes with one click in the console — it doesn't silently degrade or spill over to other projects.

posts.title: ReAct: Teaching LLM Agents to Think, Then Act
posts.subtitle: Pure reasoning hallucinates. Pure acting flails. Interleaving the two is what makes an agent reliable.
posts.summary: ReAct interleaves short bursts of reasoning ('Thought') with concrete tool calls ('Action') and their real-world results ('Observation'), looping until the model has enough grounded evidence to answer. It's the pattern underneath most modern LLM agent frameworks, and it trades extra tokens and latency for far fewer confidently-wrong answers.

slides.title: Two Ways for an Agent to Fail, and One Fix
slides.body: An LLM that only reasons can talk itself into a wrong answer with total confidence. An LLM that only acts repeats failed tool calls without noticing. ReAct interleaves the two.
bullets: Short for 'Reasoning and Acting'
Core loop: Thought → Action → Observation → repeat → Answer

slides.title: Chain-of-Thought Alone Can't Check Its Own Work
slides.body: Chain-of-thought prompting is great at laying out multi-step logic, but every fact in that chain comes from the model's own weights — there's no way to verify a claim mid-reasoning.
bullets: A single wrong fact early in the chain poisons every step after it
The model has no mechanism to say 'let me check' — it can only keep reasoning from what it already believes

Meanwhile an act-only agent (tool calls with no reflection) has the opposite problem: it can look things up, but doesn't notice when a result is irrelevant or contradicts the goal, so it repeats the same failed action or drifts off-task

slides.title: The Loop: Thought, Action, Observation
slides.body: Each step of a ReAct trace has three parts, and the model generates all three in its own output before the next tool call runs.
bullets: Thought: a short note on what's still missing and what to try next ('I need the founding year, let me search for it')
Action: a structured call to a real tool — search, a calculator, a database query, an API
Observation: the tool's actual return value, inserted back into context before the next Thought
The loop repeats until a Thought concludes the model has enough grounded evidence, then it emits a final Answer action

slides.title: Example: 'Which of these two laptops is cheaper after tax?'
slides.body: A typical trace makes the interleaving concrete:
bullets: Thought: I need both prices and the local tax rate before I can compare — search for laptop A's price.
Action: search("Laptop A price")  →  Observation: "$899"
Thought: Now I need Laptop B's price.  Action: search("Laptop B price")  →  Observation: "$949"
Thought: Laptop A is cheaper before tax, and tax is a flat percentage, so it stays cheaper after tax — no need to search for the tax rate at all. Answer: Laptop A.

slides.title: Reasoning Alone vs. Acting Alone vs. ReAct
slides.body: Each approach fails in a different place — which is exactly why interleaving them covers more ground than either one.

rows: No way to verify a claim — confidently wrong answers
Repeats failed actions, loses track of the actual goal
Reasons about what's missing, then verifies it
Extra Thought tokens add latency and cost per step

slides.title: When ReAct Isn't the Right Tool
slides.body: Interleaving reasoning and acting isn't free, and it isn't always necessary.
bullets: Simple single-tool lookups (one API call, no ambiguity) don't need a reasoning loop — it's pure overhead
Long traces accumulate Thought/Action/Observation text in context, which increases both cost and the chance an early mistake gets carried forward uncorrected
Models that weren't tuned or few-shot-prompted for the Thought/Action/Observation format tend to produce sloppy, rambling thoughts that don't actually constrain the next action
It still inherits chain-of-thought's weakness within each Thought step — reasoning about an observation can itself be wrong, it's just now checked against reality one step sooner

slides.title: Why It's the Default Agent Pattern
slides.body: Nearly every modern agent framework — LangChain's agent executors, early AutoGPT-style loops, tool-calling APIs — is some variation of this same Thought/Action/Observation cycle.
bullets: Reasoning without acting hallucinates; acting without reasoning flails — ReAct's loop grounds each reasoning step in a real result
The pattern composes with memory and context engineering: observations are exactly the kind of fresh, high-value tokens worth keeping in context
Use it when a task needs multiple dependent lookups or decisions; skip it for single-call, unambiguous tool use

questions.prompt: What are the three repeating steps in the ReAct loop?
options: Plan, Execute, Review
Thought, Action, Observation
Search, Rank, Generate
Encode, Retrieve, Decode
questions.explanation: ReAct repeats Thought (what's missing / what to try) → Action (a real tool call) → Observation (the tool's actual result) until it has enough grounded evidence to answer.

questions.prompt: Why does a pure chain-of-thought model risk confidently wrong answers?
options: It uses too many tokens per step
It can only run one tool at a time
Every fact in the chain comes from its own weights, with no way to verify a claim mid-reasoning
It can't produce more than one sentence per step
questions.explanation: Without a way to check facts against the outside world, chain-of-thought just keeps reasoning from whatever it already 'believes,' so one wrong early fact propagates uncorrected through the rest of the chain.

questions.prompt: What's a real downside of ReAct compared to a single direct tool call?
options: It cannot use external tools at all
It requires no prompting or tuning to work well
The extra Thought steps add latency and token cost, and aren't worth it for simple single-lookup tasks
It only works with search engines, never databases or calculators
questions.explanation: Every Thought adds tokens and a round-trip before the next Action — fine for multi-step tasks that need re-evaluation, but pure overhead for a task that's really just one unambiguous tool call.

posts.title: RoPE: Encoding Position by Rotating Vectors
posts.subtitle: How rotary embeddings give attention relative position for free
posts.summary: Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) encode a token's position by rotating its query and key vectors through an angle proportional to that position. The rotation's key property — the resulting attention score depends only on the distance between two tokens, not their absolute positions — is why RoPE became the default in modern LLMs, and why it needs extra scaling tricks to handle context lengths it wasn't trained on.

slides.title: Position, Encoded as a Rotation
bullets: No position embedding table, no bias term added to attention scores
Just: rotate Q and K before the dot product

slides.body: Self-attention computes a weighted sum over all tokens using dot products of query and key vectors. Swap two tokens' positions and the raw dot products don't change — attention is permutation-invariant by construction. Something has to inject 'where' each token sits, or the model can't tell 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'.
slides.title: Attention Has No Sense of Order on Its Own
bullets: Original Transformer fix: add a fixed sinusoidal vector per position to the input
BERT/GPT-2 fix: a learned embedding table, one row per position — capped at the trained max length

slides.body: RoPE splits each query/key vector into 2D pairs of dimensions. For a token at position m, each pair is rotated by an angle m·θ_i, where θ_i shrinks geometrically across dimension-pairs i (θ_i = base^(-2i/d), base is typically 10000+). Low-frequency pairs rotate slowly and capture long-range position; high-frequency pairs rotate fast and capture fine-grained local position.
slides.title: Rotate Instead of Add
bullets: Applied only to Q and K — never to V
No extra parameters: it's a deterministic rotation matrix, not a learned table
Composes cleanly with KV caching since each cached key keeps a fixed rotation

slides.body: Rotating both q at position m and k at position n by m·θ and n·θ means their dot product depends only on (m − n)·θ — the rotation angles subtract out everything except the relative distance. Two tokens 50 apart produce the identical positional contribution to attention whether they sit at positions (2, 52) or (9000, 9050).
slides.title: The Property That Makes It Work: Relativity for Free
bullets: No explicit relative-position lookup table needed — relativity falls out of the rotation algebra
This is the core reason RoPE generalizes better than naively-added absolute embeddings

slides.body: Take one frequency with θ = 0.01 rad per position step. Tokens at positions 2 and 5 rotate by 0.02 and 0.05 rad — a 0.03 rad gap. Tokens at positions 9002 and 9005 rotate by 90.02 and 90.05 rad — still a 0.03 rad gap. The attention contribution from that frequency is identical in both cases, because only the gap survives in the dot product, not the absolute rotation amount.
slides.title: Worked Example: Same Gap, Same Angle
bullets: This is why a model can in principle recognize 'two tokens 3 apart' anywhere in a long sequence
In practice it only holds reliably up to roughly the context length the model was trained on

rows: Good, up to the scaled target length

slides.title: RoPE vs. the Alternatives

slides.body: Push a vanilla-RoPE model past its trained context length and quality collapses: the model is now seeing rotation angles it never encountered during training, effectively out-of-distribution inputs to the attention dot product. The fix isn't retraining — it's rescaling the rotation frequencies (NTK-aware scaling, YaRN, or position interpolation) so familiar-looking angles cover a longer range.
slides.title: Where Vanilla RoPE Breaks — and the Fix
bullets: Symptom: fluent output degrades sharply past the trained length, not gracefully
Fix class: stretch or interpolate θ_i so the model reuses angle ranges it already learned
Tradeoff: most scaling methods trade a little short-context precision for long-context stability

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: RoPE rotates Q and K in 2D sub-planes by an angle proportional to position — no learned table, no added bias
Rotating both vectors makes their dot product depend only on relative distance, which is what actually encodes 'position' to attention
Vanilla RoPE still degrades past its trained context length — that's what NTK-aware scaling and YaRN exist to fix
It's the de facto default in modern LLMs because it's parameter-free, relative by construction, and KV-cache-friendly

questions.explanation: RoPE is applied to Q and K before the attention dot product; V is left untouched, so the rotated positional signal only affects how much attention a token gets, not what value it carries.
questions.prompt: What does RoPE actually rotate?
options: The value (V) vectors only
The query and key (Q and K) vectors, in 2D sub-planes
The final output logits
The token embedding table itself, permanently

questions.explanation: Rotating q at position m and k at position n by m·θ and n·θ leaves only (m−n)·θ in their dot product — the absolute positions cancel out, leaving pure relative distance.
questions.prompt: Why does rotating Q and K by position-dependent angles encode relative position?
options: Because the rotation angles are learned from data
Because the dot product of two rotated vectors depends only on the difference between their rotation angles, i.e. their position gap
Because rotation increases the vector's magnitude proportional to position
It doesn't — RoPE still needs a separate relative-position bias term

questions.explanation: Rotation angles beyond the trained range are angles the model never learned to interpret, so attention quality drops sharply — scaling methods rescale θ so the model reuses familiar angle ranges for longer sequences.
questions.prompt: What happens when a vanilla-RoPE model is run on sequences longer than its training context, and what fixes it?
options: Nothing — RoPE extrapolates perfectly by construction
It runs out of memory immediately; the fix is quantization
Quality degrades because the model sees out-of-distribution rotation angles; the fix is frequency rescaling like NTK-aware scaling or YaRN
It silently truncates the input with no quality change

posts.title: Agent Skills Moves to the Linux Foundation
posts.subtitle: Anthropic hands the open skill standard to a vendor-neutral home
posts.summary: Anthropic donated Agent Skills — the open SKILL.md standard for giving agents specialized know-how — to the Agentic AI Foundation, a Linux Foundation project that already hosts MCP. The standard already spans 70+ platforms, 1M published skills, and ~280M installs, and governance now sits with individual maintainers across companies instead of one vendor.

slides.title: A Skill Format Just Left Its Creator's Control
bullets: Oct 22, 2026: Anthropic donates Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)
AAIF is a Linux Foundation project — and it already hosts MCP

slides.body: Agent Skills launched from Anthropic in October 2025 and was published as an open spec that December. But a format for 'how agents carry specialized knowledge' that lives under one company's GitHub org creates an obvious conflict: why would a competing platform build deep dependencies on infrastructure a rival controls?
slides.title: A Standard Owned by One Vendor Is a Standard Nobody Fully Trusts
bullets: 70+ platforms had already adopted Skills — including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code
That adoption outpaced the governance model: single-vendor ownership of a cross-platform standard

slides.title: What Actually Changed Hands
bullets: The Agent Skills name, logo, GitHub org, and the agentskills.io domain all transfer to AAIF
Lead maintainers (David Soria Parra, Mahesh Murag) now act as individuals, not company representatives
Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and others maintain the spec jointly
AAIF was co-founded by Anthropic, Block, and OpenAI — and Anthropic donated MCP to it earlier too

slides.body: A Skill is a directory containing a SKILL.md file plus whatever scripts or reference material the task needs. The SKILL.md carries the instructions an agent reads; the surrounding files are the tools it can reach for. That simplicity is exactly why a one-vendor format could spread to 70+ unrelated platforms — there's almost nothing proprietary to lock in.
slides.title: A Skill Is Just a Folder — That's the Whole Trick
bullets: SKILL.md = instructions and metadata an agent loads
Supporting scripts/resources = the actual capability the skill grants

slides.title: The Scale That Forced the Governance Question

slides.body: Say a developer writes a 'generate-changelog' skill for Claude Code: a SKILL.md plus a small script that diffs commits into release notes. Because the format is now a neutral standard with 70+ adopters, that same folder can run unmodified in GitHub Copilot or Cursor — no per-platform rewrite, and no risk that the format's rules change at one vendor's discretion.
slides.title: Why a Cursor User Should Care
bullets: One skill folder, many agent platforms, zero platform-specific forking
Governance change doesn't touch the file format — existing skills keep working as-is

slides.body: Vendor-neutral governance isn't the same as quality control. The roadmap AAIF proposes — versioned releases, a formal change process, security guidance for installing third-party skills — is still just a roadmap, not shipped tooling. With ~1M skills already published under the old, looser process, security review for untrusted skills remains an open problem, not a solved one.
slides.title: What Donation Doesn't Fix
bullets: Security guidance for installing skills is 'proposed', not yet delivered
Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI co-founding AAIF means influence is shared, not absent
Nothing is required of current users — you can keep using the standard without joining AAIF

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Agent Skills (SKILL.md + scripts) is now governed by the Agentic AI Foundation, a Linux Foundation project — not by Anthropic alone
This follows the same path as MCP, which Anthropic donated to AAIF earlier
The format already reached 70+ platforms, ~1M published skills, and ~280M installs before the handoff
Nothing changes for existing users today — the shift is about who steers the spec next, not the file format itself
